opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the biggest thing is just how much they moved in one year. We asked basically the same questions in 2022 and 2023, and the aggregate forecast for when "high-level machine intelligence" arrives (unaided machines that can do every task better and more cheaply than human workers) moved from about 2060 to about 2047. That's roughly thirteen years earlier, in a single year. In earlier rounds, between 2016 and 2022, things had barely moved, so this was a real break.

The forecast for full automation of labor moved even more, something like forty-eight years earlier. It went from the 2160s to around 2116. Of course it's still strange that those two numbers are so far apart. Logically, if machines can do every task better and more cheaply, it's hard to see why it would take another seventy years for all occupations to be automatable. So I'd be careful not to treat any single number as a precise belief. People answer differently depending on how you frame the question, and that framing sensitivity is itself one of the most robust findings we have.

Still, the direction is very clear. This was right after ChatGPT and GPT-4, and I think a lot of researchers updated on seeing those systems in person. It's interesting that the experts' sense of things is quite responsive to what they're seeing, rather than being anchored on a fixed view. It also means that if you'd treated the 2022 numbers as the settled expert consensus, you'd have been quite wrong a year later. That suggests some humility about how stable these forecasts are.

The other thing I'd flag is the spread. There's huge disagreement among individual respondents. A meaningful fraction think something like this is plausible within the next ten years or so, and others think it's centuries away. So the aggregate shifting earlier doesn't mean everyone converged. The whole distribution slid earlier, and it's still very wide.

r001.rationale: It says HLMI shifted about 13 years earlier, while full labor automation shifted about 48 years earlier.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the 2022–2023 shift with earlier rounds from 2016 to 2022, when forecasts had barely moved.

r003.rationale: It gives the forecast calendar years (about 2060 to 2047 and the 2160s to 2116) and describes the changes as years earlier.

fable-5.1.text:
Katja Grace: The most striking thing is just how much the timelines moved in a single year. We ran the 2022 survey and then the 2023 survey a bit over a year apart, and normally when we've done these surveys, the aggregate predictions shift a little, maybe a few years here or there. This time, the aggregate forecast for when AI could outperform humans at every task, what we call high-level machine intelligence, came in something like thirteen years earlier than it had the year before. For the fifty percent probability point, it went from roughly 2060 to roughly 2047. And for full automation of all human occupations, the drop was even bigger, something like forty-eight years earlier, though that question has always produced much later estimates for reasons we don't fully understand.

What I find notable isn't only the size of the shift, it's what it says about how people form these views. These are hundreds, in fact thousands, of researchers who published at top machine learning venues, and a single year of progress, basically the arrival of ChatGPT and GPT-4, moved their expectations more than the previous six years of surveys combined. That suggests to me that people weren't really extrapolating from a stable model of progress beforehand. They were updating pretty heavily on salient recent events. You can read that charitably, as researchers appropriately responding to evidence, or less charitably, as evidence that nobody has a very principled way of forecasting this and everyone is reacting to vibes.

The other thing I'd point out is the detail underneath the headline numbers. The near-term predictions for specific milestones also moved earlier, things like writing a New York Times bestseller, or writing simple Python code from instructions, which several respondents now thought was already feasible. And at the same time, the distribution stayed extremely wide. There's still a substantial chunk of respondents putting real probability mass beyond the end of the century, and the median person gives a nontrivial chance to things happening within the next decade. So the picture is one of a field that collectively moved toward "sooner" but still really disagrees with itself, and I think the honest reading is a lot of uncertainty rather than a confident consensus that it's close.

r001.rationale: It says the HLMI forecast moved about 13 years earlier, while the full-automation forecast moved about 48 years earlier.

r002.rationale: It says the 2022–2023 shift exceeded the changes across the previous six years of surveys combined, indicating relative stability over that earlier period.

r003.rationale: It gives HLMI forecast calendar years of roughly 2060 and 2047, making clear that the reported change is in predicted dates.

astra-6.text:
The striking thing is how much they moved in just one year. In the 2022 survey, the aggregate forecast put a 50 percent chance of machines outperforming humans at every task around 2060. In 2023, that moved to around 2047—a thirteen-year shift.

I wouldn’t interpret that as a precise countdown. These forecasts are quite sensitive to how you ask the question, and there’s a lot of disagreement among researchers. But it is notable that a large group of people working in AI revised their expectations that substantially over such a short period. It suggests that the developments in that year changed their picture of what was plausible, rather than just confirming the trajectory they already expected.

r001.rationale: It gives a shift in the forecast for machines outperforming humans at every task, but does not compare that shift with forecasts for full labor automation.

r002.rationale: It compares the 2022 and 2023 HLMI forecasts, but says nothing about their stability from 2016 to 2022.

r003.rationale: It identifies the estimates as years—around 2060 and around 2047—so the decrease is clearly in predicted calendar years.

sol-6.1.text:
The striking thing was how much the forecasts moved in just one year. In the 2022 survey, the aggregate forecast put a 50 percent chance of machines outperforming humans at every task around 2060. In 2023, that had moved to around 2047—a thirteen-year shift between surveys conducted only a year apart.

I wouldn’t interpret that as a precise countdown. These forecasts are very uncertain, and the way you ask the question matters quite a lot. But it is a substantial update toward shorter timelines from the researchers themselves, during a period when people were seeing some pretty surprising progress in AI.

r001.rationale: It reports a shift from 2060 to 2047 for machines outperforming humans at every task, but does not compare that shift with the change in full labor automation predictions.

r002.rationale: It describes the 2022–2023 shift but does not contrast it with HLMI predictions’ relative stability from 2016 to 2022.

r003.rationale: It gives predicted years and the size of the shift, but does not clarify that the decreases are in calendar years rather than years remaining.
